items.title: The lobotomy was awarded a Nobel Prize
items.claim: Egas Moniz won the 1949 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discovery of the therapeutic value of the prefrontal leucotomy (lobotomy). What's the modern status?

options.text: The procedure remains a first-line treatment

Lobotomy is no longer performed; thousands of patients (around 40,000-50,000 in the US alone, 1936-50s) suffered permanent personality damage. Modern psychosurgery is far more targeted (deep brain stimulation, cingulotomy for refractory OCD)

items.reveal_title: An honoured procedure that caused immense harm
items.reveal:
Walter Freeman performed perhaps 3,500 of his transorbital 'icepick' lobotomies in the US through the 1950s. Patients included Rosemary Kennedy (1941, permanently incapacitated) and many institutionalised individuals.

The procedure declined rapidly after chlorpromazine (1952) provided pharmacological alternatives. Calls to revoke Moniz's Nobel continue. Modern functional neurosurgery (capsulotomy, cingulotomy, deep brain stimulation) targets specific circuits with imaging guidance and is reversible (in DBS).
items.why: Therapeutic enthusiasm without rigorous evidence can produce widespread harm. Modern evidence-based standards exist because of cases like this.

items.title: Deinstitutionalisation reduced asylum populations dramatically
items.claim: Following Italy's Basaglia Law (1978), the UK's Care in the Community policy (1980s-90s) and similar reforms elsewhere, what happened to inpatient psychiatric populations?

options.text: Inpatient populations fell by 60-90% in most Western countries by 2000. Outcomes were mixed: better integration for many, but inadequate community resources left some patients homeless or in the criminal justice system
Inpatient care was completely eliminated everywhere

items.reveal:
UK psychiatric inpatient beds: ~150,000 in 1955, ~22,000 by 2010. The shift was driven by both ideology (asylum critique, e.g. Goffman 'Asylums' 1961) and pharmacology (chlorpromazine, 1952).

Where community resources followed (Trieste, Italy under Basaglia), outcomes were generally positive. Where they didn't (UK and US in different ways), gaps in care emerged — over-representation of severely mentally ill people in prisons and homelessness is widely documented.
items.why: Major mental health policy changes have decades-long consequences. The reduction in coercive asylum care was widely accepted; the under-investment in community alternatives is the unresolved part.

items.title: Growth mindset meta-analyses
items.claim: Carol Dweck's growth mindset theory inspired large-scale school interventions. What did Sisk et al.'s 2018 meta-analysis report about the effect on academic achievement?

options.text: Very large positive effects in all settings
Small effects on average, larger for at-risk students

items.reveal:
Sisk et al. (2018) found a weak overall correlation between mindset and achievement, with stronger effects among lower-attaining and at-risk groups.

A 2019 US national experiment (Yeager et al.) found small but real gains for lower-achieving high schoolers.
items.why: Educational interventions rarely produce uniform effects across populations.
